title: Perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Since elementary cellular automata whose behavior looks complex can do computations as sophisticated as desired, they are expected to be universal, so perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And this suggests that such cellular automata will in the end turn out to be universal—with the result that out of the 256 elementary rules one expects that perhaps as many as 27 will in fact be universal.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 11, “The Notion of Computation”; section “The Threshold of Universality in Cellular Automata” (from p. 694), p. 705. Scope: the 256 elementary cellular automata

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch11-26: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.57

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The finite domain is fully known, but the decisive property is not computably settled by ordinary enumeration. Substantial new proofs are needed for many rules.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For each symmetry-identified elementary rule counted among the 27 candidates, provide a universality proof or a nonuniversality proof and count the universal rules. The numerical prediction is supported if the final count accords with the stated upper estimate.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Finite behavioral complexity does not establish universality.

Most candidate rules lack universality or nonuniversality proofs.

The phrase 'perhaps as many as' is a weak decision target.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The candidate pool of complex-looking elementary rules can be recounted by simulation, and four rules in the symmetry class of rule 110 are known to be universal. The other candidates do not have finished proofs, so the number that are in fact universal is not determined. Existing resources fix a short list and a lower bound, not the count in the claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: List the elementary rules whose typical behavior is not periodic or nested, and ask which of them emulate a Turing machine. The numerical claim is confirmed if the number of universal elementary rules is about 27, and refuted if a completed classification puts the number far from 27.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Perhaps as many as is a hedged count, so only a classification far from 27 is a clear refutation.

Looking complex, and emulating one step of every elementary rule, does not prove universality.
